title: Part I: Dissolution of Partnership Firm

topics.title: Dissolution of partnership vs dissolution of firm

learn.hook: A partner retires and the shop stays open – or the shutters come down for good. Both are 'dissolution', but they are very different.
points: Dissolution of partnership: the existing agreement ends and a new one is formed (e.g. on admission, retirement, death or change in ratio); the firm continues.
Dissolution of firm: the partnership among ALL partners ends; business stops, assets are sold and liabilities paid, and the books are closed.
Dissolution of a firm always dissolves the partnership, but dissolution of partnership does not necessarily dissolve the firm.
Differences: continuation of business, court intervention (possible only for dissolution of firm), settlement of assets and liabilities, and closure of books.

example.q: Ravi, Sana and Joseph run a café. Joseph retires; Ravi and Sana carry on. Later the café closes and everything is sold. Classify each event.
steps: Joseph's retirement: agreement ends, business continues → dissolution of partnership.
Closing the café, selling assets and paying debts → dissolution of firm.
example.answer: Retirement = dissolution of partnership; closure = dissolution of firm.

learn.reallife: Many small partnership firms during the COVID-19 lockdowns in India had to choose between reconstituting with fewer partners and dissolving the firm entirely.

quiz.q: Dissolution of partnership means:
options: a change in the existing relationship among partners while the business may continue
closing the business completely
selling all the firm's assets
conversion of the firm into a company
quiz.explain: The old agreement ends and a new one forms; the firm can carry on.
steps: Dissolution of partnership ends the old agreement and forms a new one.
The business may continue, e.g. on admission or retirement.
Answer: a change in the existing relationship among partners while the business may continue
quiz.mistake: Thinks every dissolution closes the business

quiz.q: Dissolution of a firm means:
options: only one partner leaves
the partnership among all partners ends and the business is closed
the profit-sharing ratio changes
a new partner is admitted
quiz.explain: All partners part ways; assets are realised, debts paid and books closed.
steps: Dissolution of a firm ends the partnership among all partners.
Business closes, assets are sold, debts paid and books closed.
Answer: the partnership among all partners ends and the business is closed
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with reconstitution

quiz.q: Which event is a dissolution of PARTNERSHIP but not of the firm?
options: All partners becoming insolvent
The business becoming illegal
Retirement of a partner while the others continue the business
Partners agreeing to close down
quiz.explain: On retirement, the agreement ends but the business carries on.
steps: On retirement, the agreement ends but the others carry on the business.
So it is dissolution of partnership, not of the firm.
All partners insolvent, illegal business or agreeing to close end the firm.
Answer: Retirement of a partner while the others continue the business
quiz.mistake: Picks an event that ends the firm

quiz.q: On dissolution of a firm, which account is prepared to sell assets and pay liabilities?
options: Revaluation Account
Profit and Loss Appropriation Account
Profit and Loss Suspense Account
Realisation Account
quiz.explain: A Realisation Account records the sale of assets and payment of liabilities.
steps: On dissolution of a firm, assets are sold and liabilities paid.
These are recorded in the Realisation Account.
Revaluation is used on reconstitution.
Answer: Realisation Account
quiz.mistake: Confuses realisation with revaluation

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Dissolution of a firm necessarily involves dissolution of the partnership.
Reason (R): When the firm is dissolved, the relationship among all the partners comes to an end.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Once the firm ends, no partnership remains among any partners; R explains A.
steps: A: dissolving a firm always dissolves the partnership – true.
R: when the firm ends, relations among all partners end – true.
That is why A follows.
So both are true and R correctly explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Thinks the two are independent

quiz.q: In which case are the books of account closed?
options: Dissolution of partnership on admission
Dissolution of firm
Change in profit-sharing ratio
Retirement of a partner
quiz.explain: Only when the firm itself ends are all accounts settled and closed.
steps: Books are closed only when the firm itself ends.
Admission, retirement and ratio changes continue the books.
Answer: Dissolution of firm
quiz.mistake: Thinks books close on every reconstitution

quiz.q: Court intervention is possible in:
options: admission of a partner
change in profit-sharing ratio
dissolution of a firm
every retirement of a partner
quiz.explain: A court can order dissolution of a firm on certain grounds; reconstitution is by agreement.
steps: A court can order dissolution of a firm on certain grounds.
Reconstitutions are by agreement, without a court.
Answer: dissolution of a firm
quiz.mistake: Thinks courts handle routine reconstitution

quiz.q: Assets and liabilities are revalued in dissolution of partnership, but in dissolution of a firm they are:
options: revalued and kept in the books
transferred to the new partner
ignored
realised (sold) and settled
quiz.explain: A dissolved firm sells its assets and pays off its liabilities.
steps: In dissolution of a firm, assets are sold and liabilities paid.
So they are realised and settled, not revalued and kept.
Answer: realised (sold) and settled
quiz.mistake: Mixes up revaluation with realisation

teach.ask: Gappu thinks retirement and closing the firm are the same. Explain the difference.
teach.praise: Exactly! Dissolution of partnership changes the agreement; dissolution of firm closes the business.
teach.nudge: Gappu asks: in which case does the business carry on?

revise.summary: Dissolution of partnership ends the old agreement while the firm may continue; dissolution of the firm ends the partnership among all partners, closes the business, realises assets, pays liabilities and closes the books.
focus: Dissolution of partnership vs dissolution of firm
Examples of each
Bases of difference: business, court, settlement, books
remember: Dissolution of firm always dissolves the partnership, not vice versa
Retirement, admission, death, change in ratio → dissolution of partnership
Firm dissolved → Realisation Account
traps: Retirement of one partner does not dissolve the firm if others continue
Court intervention applies to dissolution of firm
Revaluation is for reconstitution; realisation is for dissolution

topics.title: Modes of dissolution of a firm

learn.hook: Firms can end by choice, by law, by circumstance, by a letter, or by a judge's order. Know all five doors out.
points: By agreement (Sec 40): with the consent of all partners, or as per a contract among them.
Compulsory dissolution (Sec 41): when all partners or all but one become insolvent, or the business becomes unlawful.
On certain contingencies (Sec 42), subject to contract: expiry of the fixed term, completion of the venture, death of a partner, or insolvency of a partner.
By notice (Sec 43): in a partnership at will, any partner may give written notice to all others of his intention to dissolve.

By court (Sec 44), on a partner's suit: unsound mind, permanent incapacity, misconduct affecting the business, persistent breach of agreement, transfer of whole interest to a third party, business can be carried on only at a loss, or just and equitable grounds.

example.q: Three partners formed a firm only to organise a trade fair in Pragati Maidan. The fair is over. What happens to the firm?
steps: The firm was formed for a particular venture.
On completion of the venture, the firm is dissolved on the happening of a contingency (unless the partners agree otherwise).
example.answer: It is dissolved on completion of the venture (Section 42).

learn.reallife: If a government ban makes a product illegal – as happened with some single-use plastics in India – a firm dealing only in it faces compulsory dissolution.

quiz.q: A firm is dissolved when its business becomes unlawful. This is:
options: compulsory dissolution
dissolution by agreement
dissolution by notice
dissolution by court
quiz.explain: Section 41 dissolves a firm automatically if the business becomes illegal.
steps: Section 41: compulsory dissolution when all (or all but one) partners are insolvent or the business becomes unlawful.
So an unlawful business means compulsory dissolution.
Answer: compulsory dissolution
quiz.mistake: Thinks the partners must agree first

quiz.q: A partnership at will can be dissolved by:
options: only a court order
any partner giving written notice to all other partners
only the death of a partner
a public advertisement by the firm
quiz.explain: In a partnership at will, written notice by a partner is enough (Section 43).
steps: Section 43: in a partnership at will, any partner may give written notice to all others.
So written notice dissolves it.
Answer: any partner giving written notice to all other partners
quiz.mistake: Thinks a court order is needed

quiz.q: Which is a ground on which the COURT may dissolve a firm?
options: The firm has completed its fixed term
All partners agree to dissolve
A partner has become of unsound mind
All partners have become insolvent
quiz.explain: Unsound mind is a Section 44 ground; the others dissolve the firm without a court.
steps: Section 44 court grounds include unsound mind, incapacity, misconduct, breach, transfer of interest, losses.
Fixed term, agreement and insolvency of all dissolve without a court.
So unsound mind is the court ground.
Answer: A partner has become of unsound mind
quiz.mistake: Mixes up contingencies with court grounds

quiz.q: A firm formed for 5 years reaches the end of its term. It is dissolved:
options: compulsorily by law
only by a court order
only if a partner gives notice
on the happening of a contingency, subject to any contract between partners
quiz.explain: Expiry of a fixed term is a contingency under Section 42.
steps: Section 42: expiry of a fixed term is a contingency.
The firm is dissolved on it, subject to any contract between partners.
Answer: on the happening of a contingency, subject to any contract between partners
quiz.mistake: Thinks it is compulsory dissolution

quiz.q: Compulsory dissolution takes place when:
options: all partners, or all but one, are declared insolvent
one partner wants to leave
a partner dies
the firm earns a low profit
quiz.explain: Insolvency of all (or all but one) partners leaves no one able to contract, so the firm is dissolved under Section 41.
steps: Section 41: compulsory dissolution when all partners, or all but one, are insolvent.
One partner leaving or dying is not compulsory dissolution.
Answer: all partners, or all but one, are declared insolvent
quiz.mistake: Thinks death of one partner is compulsory dissolution

quiz.q: A partner transfers his whole interest in the firm to an outsider. The other partners may:
options: dissolve the firm automatically
apply to the court for dissolution
seize his private property
expel him without any process
quiz.explain: Transfer of whole interest to a third party is a ground for dissolution by the court.
steps: Transfer of a partner's whole interest to an outsider is a Section 44 ground.
So the others may apply to the court for dissolution.
Answer: apply to the court for dissolution
quiz.mistake: Thinks the firm ends automatically

quiz.q: Dissolution by agreement can happen:
options: only when a court orders
only when the firm makes losses
with the consent of all the partners or under a contract among them
only when a partner dies
quiz.explain: Section 40 allows dissolution by mutual consent or contract.
steps: Section 40: dissolution by agreement, with the consent of all partners or as per a contract.
Answer: with the consent of all the partners or under a contract among them
quiz.mistake: Thinks consent of the majority is enough

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a ground for dissolution by court?
options: Persistent breach of the partnership agreement
Misconduct of a partner affecting the business
Business can be carried on only at a loss
A partner takes a two-week holiday
quiz.explain: A short holiday is not misconduct or incapacity.
steps: Court grounds: unsound mind, incapacity, misconduct, persistent breach, transfer of interest, loss-only business, just and equitable grounds.
A two-week holiday is none of these.
Answer: A partner takes a two-week holiday
quiz.mistake: Treats any absence as a legal ground

teach.ask: Gappu wants to know all the ways a firm can be dissolved. Teach him.
teach.praise: Superb! Agreement, compulsory, contingency, notice and court – Gappu knows every exit.
teach.nudge: Gappu asks: can a court order a firm to be dissolved? On what grounds?

revise.summary: A firm may be dissolved by agreement (Sec 40), compulsorily (Sec 41), on contingencies like expiry of term, completion of venture, death or insolvency (Sec 42), by notice in a partnership at will (Sec 43) or by the court (Sec 44).
focus: The five modes and their sections
Grounds for dissolution by court
Matching a case to the mode
remember: Sec 40: agreement
Sec 41: compulsory – all or all but one insolvent, or business unlawful
Sec 42: contingencies; Sec 43: notice (partnership at will)
Sec 44: court
traps: Insolvency of all partners is compulsory dissolution, not dissolution by court
Expiry of a fixed term is a contingency (Sec 42)
A short absence is not a ground for court dissolution

learn.hook: When a firm closes, there's a strict queue for the money. Outsiders first, partners' loans next, capitals after that.
points: Losses, including deficiencies of capital, are paid first out of profits, then out of capital, and lastly by partners individually in their profit-sharing ratio.

Assets (including sums contributed by partners) are applied in this order: (i) debts of the firm to third parties; (ii) partners' loans/advances (as distinct from capital); (iii) partners' capitals; (iv) any surplus is shared in the profit-sharing ratio.
Private assets and liabilities (Sec 49): firm's property goes first to firm's debts; a partner's private property goes first to his private debts, and any surplus may be used for the firm's debts.
This course excludes piecemeal distribution, sale of the firm to a company and insolvency of partners.

example.q: On dissolution, a firm has ₹3,00,000 after selling assets. Creditors are owed ₹1,80,000 and partner A's loan is ₹40,000. Partners' capitals total ₹1,00,000. How is the cash used?
steps: Pay creditors first: ₹1,80,000 → ₹1,20,000 left.
Pay A's loan next: ₹40,000 → ₹80,000 left.
Capitals of ₹1,00,000 can be paid only ₹80,000; the ₹20,000 shortfall is a loss shared in the profit-sharing ratio.
example.answer: Creditors → A's loan → capitals; ₹20,000 loss shared by partners in profit-sharing ratio.

learn.reallife: Like passengers stepping off an Indian Railways coach in order, claims are settled strictly: outside creditors, then partners' loans, then capitals.

quiz.explain: Outside creditors rank first.

So debts of the firm to third parties are paid first.
Answer: Debts of the firm to third parties

quiz.q: After paying outside creditors, the next payment is:
options: partners' capitals
partners' loans and advances
realisation expenses of the previous year
surplus in profit-sharing ratio
quiz.explain: Loans by partners rank after outside debts but before capitals.
steps: After outside creditors come partners' loans and advances.
Capitals come after loans.
Answer: partners' loans and advances
quiz.mistake: Pays capitals before loans

quiz.q: Cash available ₹3,00,000; creditors ₹1,80,000; A's loan ₹40,000; capitals total ₹1,00,000. Loss to be borne by partners:
quiz.explain: After creditors and A's loan, ₹80,000 remains for ₹1,00,000 of capitals – a shortfall of ₹20,000.
steps: Answer: ₹20,000
quiz.mistake: Treats A's loan as capital

quiz.q: Losses on dissolution, including deficiency of capital, are borne by partners:
options: in their capital ratio
equally always
in the ratio of their loans
in their profit-sharing ratio
quiz.explain: Section 48 says losses are made good by partners in the ratio in which they share profits.
steps: Section 48: losses, including capital deficiency, are borne by partners in their profit-sharing ratio.
Answer: in their profit-sharing ratio
quiz.mistake: Uses the capital ratio

quiz.q: Under Section 49, a partner's private property is applied:
options: first to his private debts; any surplus can go towards the firm's debts
first to the firm's debts
only to the firm's debts
equally to private and firm's debts
quiz.explain: Private assets serve private creditors first.
steps: Section 49: private property goes first to private debts.
Any surplus may go towards the firm's debts.
Answer: first to his private debts; any surplus can go towards the firm's debts
quiz.mistake: Reverses the priority

quiz.q: A partner's private creditors claim against the firm's property. Under Section 49, the firm's property is applied:
options: first to pay private debts of that partner
first to pay the firm's debts
equally to both
only after partners' capitals are paid
quiz.explain: The firm's property is first used for the firm's own debts.
steps: Section 49: the firm's property is applied first to the firm's own debts.
Private creditors come only after that.
Answer: first to pay the firm's debts
quiz.mistake: Lets private creditors jump the queue

quiz.q: Which topic is NOT part of the CBSE dissolution syllabus for this course?
options: Realisation Account
Settlement of partners' loans
Piecemeal distribution of cash
Closing partners' capital accounts
quiz.explain: Piecemeal distribution, sale to a company and insolvency of partners are excluded.
steps: Excluded from this course: piecemeal distribution, sale to a company, insolvency of partners.
So piecemeal distribution of cash is NOT in the syllabus.
Answer: Piecemeal distribution of cash
quiz.mistake: Thinks every dissolution topic is examined

quiz.q: After paying creditors, partners' loans and capitals, ₹12,000 is left. A and B share 2:1. A gets:
quiz.explain: Surplus is shared in the profit-sharing ratio: 12,000 × 2/3.
steps: Surplus is shared in the profit-sharing ratio 2:1.
Answer: ₹8,000
quiz.mistake: Shares the surplus equally

teach.ask: Gappu's firm is closing. Explain who gets paid first under Section 48.
teach.praise: Perfect order! Outsiders, then partners' loans, then capitals, and any surplus in the profit-sharing ratio.
teach.nudge: Gappu asks: is a partner's loan repaid before or after outside creditors?

revise.summary: Under Section 48, losses are met from profits, then capital, then partners in profit-sharing ratio. Assets go to outside debts, then partners' loans, then capitals, and any surplus in profit-sharing ratio. Section 49 keeps firm's and private assets for their own debts first.

How losses and capital deficiency are borne
Section 49 on private and firm's assets
remember: Order: outside creditors → partners' loans → partners' capitals → surplus in profit-sharing ratio
Losses: profit-sharing ratio
Firm's property → firm's debts first; private property → private debts first
traps: Partners' loans are paid before capitals, after outsiders
Losses are shared in profit-sharing ratio, not capital ratio
Private property does not go first to the firm's debts

learn.hook: On dissolution, every asset is sold and every outside debt paid – all through one account that tells you if the firm sold at a profit or a loss.
points: Realisation Account is a nominal account prepared on dissolution to record the sale of assets and payment of liabilities and find the profit or loss on realisation.
Debit: all assets at book value EXCEPT cash/bank and fictitious assets (e.g. advertisement suspense, P&L debit balance). Entry: Dr Realisation A/c, Cr Asset A/cs.

Credit: all outside liabilities and provisions against assets (e.g. provision for doubtful debts, accumulated depreciation). Partners' loans and capitals and reserves are NOT transferred. Entry: Dr Liability A/cs, Cr Realisation A/c.
Sale of assets: Dr Cash/Bank, Cr Realisation. Payment of liabilities: Dr Realisation, Cr Cash/Bank.
If no realisable value is given, assume tangible assets realise their book value and intangible assets (like goodwill) realise nothing.

example.q: Balance sheet of A and B (1:1): Building ₹2,00,000; Machinery ₹1,00,000; Stock ₹50,000; Debtors ₹40,000 less provision ₹2,000; Cash ₹20,000. Creditors ₹60,000; Bills payable ₹20,000; A's loan ₹30,000; General reserve ₹28,000; Capitals A ₹1,50,000, B ₹1,20,000. Which items go to the Realisation Account at book value?
steps: Debit side: Building 2,00,000; Machinery 1,00,000; Stock 50,000; Debtors 40,000 = ₹3,90,000.
Credit side: Provision 2,000; Creditors 60,000; Bills payable 20,000 = ₹82,000.
Cash stays in the Cash Account; A's loan, General reserve and capitals are not transferred.
example.answer: Assets ₹3,90,000 debited; liabilities and provision ₹82,000 credited.

learn.reallife: When a well-known Delhi bookshop closed, its stock was sold off, landlord dues paid and the remaining money split – a real-life Realisation Account.

Dr Cash A/c / Cr Stock A/c ₹45,000
Dr Cash A/c / Cr Realisation A/c ₹50,000

both at book value
furniture ₹30,000; goodwill nil
both nil
quiz.explain: Tangible assets are assumed to realise book value; intangibles realise nothing.
steps: No value given: tangible assets realise book value; intangible assets realise nothing.
So furniture ₹30,000 and goodwill nil.
Answer: furniture ₹30,000; goodwill nil

credited to Realisation Account
sold for cash
written off to partners' capitals in profit-sharing ratio, not taken to Realisation Account

teach.praise: Neat! Assets (except cash and fictitious) debited, outside liabilities credited, and the balance shows profit or loss.
teach.nudge: Gappu asks: which items are kept out of the Realisation Account?

revise.summary: The Realisation Account is debited with all assets except cash and fictitious assets, and credited with outside liabilities and provisions. Partners' loans, capitals and reserves are not transferred. Sales are credited and payments debited to it.

Totals of assets and liabilities transferred
Entries for sale of assets
Assumptions when no value is given

Credit: outside liabilities and provisions
Not transferred: cash, partners' loans, capitals, reserves, fictitious assets
traps: Don't transfer a partner's loan to Realisation
Debtors go at gross value; the provision is credited separately
Goodwill with no stated value realises nothing

topics.title: Assets and liabilities taken over; creditors accepting assets

learn.hook: A partner wants to keep the delivery van; a supplier happily takes stock instead of cash. These twists change the entries, so watch carefully.
points: Asset taken over by a partner: Dr Partner's Capital A/c, Cr Realisation A/c (at the agreed value).
Liability taken over by a partner: Dr Realisation A/c, Cr Partner's Capital A/c.
Creditor accepts an asset in full settlement: NO entry (both are already in the Realisation Account).
Creditor accepts an asset and some cash: record only the cash paid (Dr Realisation, Cr Cash). If an asset is accepted at a value in partial settlement, cash paid = liability − value of asset.
Unrecorded asset sold: Dr Cash, Cr Realisation; taken by a partner: Dr Partner's Capital, Cr Realisation. Unrecorded liability paid: Dr Realisation, Cr Cash.

topics.title: Realisation expenses and profit or loss on realisation

learn.hook: Closing down costs money – brokers, lawyers, transport. Who pays, and who finally bears it? Five cases, five different entries.
points: Expenses paid by the firm: Dr Realisation A/c, Cr Cash A/c.
Paid by a partner on behalf of the firm: Dr Realisation A/c, Cr that Partner's Capital A/c.
To be borne by a partner and paid by him: no entry. Borne by a partner but paid by the firm: Dr Partner's Capital A/c, Cr Cash A/c.
A partner is given a fixed remuneration for completing the dissolution and bears the expenses: Dr Realisation A/c, Cr Partner's Capital A/c (remuneration); no entry for the actual expenses.
Balance of Realisation: profit → Dr Realisation, Cr Partners' Capital A/cs; loss → Dr Partners' Capital A/cs, Cr Realisation; both in the profit-sharing ratio.

example.q: Balance sheet of A and B (1:1): Building ₹2,00,000; Machinery ₹1,00,000; Stock ₹50,000; Debtors ₹40,000 less provision ₹2,000; Cash ₹20,000. Creditors ₹60,000; Bills payable ₹20,000; A's loan ₹30,000; General reserve ₹28,000; Capitals A ₹1,50,000, B ₹1,20,000. Assets realise: Building ₹2,40,000, Machinery ₹80,000, Stock ₹45,000, Debtors ₹36,000. Creditors and bills payable are paid in full. Expenses ₹3,000 are paid. Find profit on realisation.
steps: Debit: assets 3,90,000 + liabilities paid 80,000 + expenses 3,000 = ₹4,73,000.
Credit: provision 2,000 + liabilities 80,000 + cash from assets 4,01,000 = ₹4,83,000.

learn.reallife: Just as a seller on an online marketplace nets the sale price minus fees, a firm's realisation profit is what's left after costs of winding up.

topics.title: Closing the books: capitals, loans and cash

learn.hook: The final scene: every account must hit zero. If the cash account balances to the last rupee, you've done the dissolution right.
points: Accumulated profits and reserves are credited, and accumulated losses and fictitious assets debited, to partners' capitals in the profit-sharing ratio.
Partner's loan is paid after outside liabilities: Dr Partner's Loan A/c, Cr Cash A/c (it does not go through Realisation).
After the realisation profit/loss is transferred, each capital account is closed: credit balance paid (Dr Capital, Cr Cash); debit balance brought in by the partner (Dr Cash, Cr Capital).
The cash/bank account closes automatically when final payments are made – total receipts equal total payments.
Key journal entries: assets/liabilities to Realisation; sale and payments; reserve distribution; loss/profit transfer; partner's loan payment; final settlement of capitals.

example.q: Balance sheet of A and B (1:1): Building ₹2,00,000; Machinery ₹1,00,000; Stock ₹50,000; Debtors ₹40,000 less provision ₹2,000; Cash ₹20,000. Creditors ₹60,000; Bills payable ₹20,000; A's loan ₹30,000; General reserve ₹28,000; Capitals A ₹1,50,000, B ₹1,20,000. Assets realise ₹4,01,000; liabilities ₹80,000 and expenses ₹3,000 are paid; profit on realisation ₹10,000. Settle the partners.
steps: Total ₹3,08,000 = cash available. The cash account closes.

learn.reallife: Like the final settlement of a closed bank account, every balance must be paid out and the books closed with nothing left over.

revise.summary: To close the books, reserves and losses go to capitals in profit-sharing ratio, partners' loans are paid after outsiders, realisation profit or loss is transferred, and capitals are settled in cash. The cash account closes with no balance.
